knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Exponential Function With a General Base

question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{ln⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}ln⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =ln⁡1-ln⁡8 \\  & =0-ln⁡8 \\  & =-ln⁡8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{ln⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{ln⁡8}+C\end{aligned}
$$

First, we factor out the constant $8.$ Then, we integrate the exponential function and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 8\cdot {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =8\int {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\cdot \frac{{5}^{x}}{\ln 5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we factor out the constant $3.$ Then, we integrate the exponential function and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3\cdot {11}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =3\int {11}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\cdot \frac{{11}^{x}}{\ln 11}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: real x; logarithmic distractors compared on x>0; arbitrary additive C

First, we factor out the constant $9.$ Then, we integrate the exponential function and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9\cdot {20}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =9\int {20}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =9\cdot \frac{{20}^{x}}{\ln 20}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: real x; logarithmic distractors compared on x>0; arbitrary additive C

First, we factor out the constant $4.$ Then, we integrate the exponential function and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4\cdot {7}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =4\int {7}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\cdot \frac{{7}^{x}}{\ln 7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: real x; logarithmic distractors compared on x>0; arbitrary additive C

First, we factor out the constant $-4.$ Then, we integrate the exponential function and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -4\cdot {13}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =-4\int {13}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4\cdot \frac{{13}^{x}}{\ln 13}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we factor out the constant $12.$ Then, we integrate the exponential function and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12\cdot {11}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =12\int {11}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =12\cdot \frac{{11}^{x}}{\ln 11}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we factor out the constant $-7.$ Then, we integrate the exponential function and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -7\cdot {17}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =-7\int {17}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-7\cdot \frac{{17}^{x}}{\ln 17}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: real x; logarithmic distractors compared on x>0; arbitrary additive C

question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}}{\ln (\frac{1}{2})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln (\frac{1}{2}) & =\ln 1-\ln 2 \\  & =0-\ln 2 \\  & =-\ln 2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}}{\ln (\frac{1}{2})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}}{\ln 2}+C\end{aligned}
$$
